title: Want, don't want, must, may
goal: Express wanting, refusing, needing, permission and obligation — five words that open up half of everyday conversation.
bekal: telling *gusto ko ng kape* from *gusto kong uminom ng kape*
knowing which words take *ko/mo/niya* and which take *ako/ka/siya*
asking permission with *puwede* without sounding pushy

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ano ang gusto mo?

notes: **Gusto has two different patterns.** If you want a **thing**, use *ng*: *gusto ko ng kape*. If you want to **do** something, use the linker: *gusto kong uminom ng kape*. Forgetting the linker in the second pattern is the most common beginner mistake you'll hear.

**Ayoko is short for ayaw ko.** The long form is still correct, but hardly anyone uses it in conversation. Note that the short form exists only for the first person: *ayaw mo*, *ayaw niya* aren't shortened.
**Gusto, ayaw and kailangan take ko/mo/niya**, while **puwede and dapat take ako/ka/siya**. There's no logic to this split; just learn it as it is — the good news is that it never changes.
**Puwede ba akong…?** is the most polite way to ask permission. The casual form is *pwede ba…?* and the shortest version that's still polite: *Pwede po?* while pointing.
**Dapat means "must" or "should"** — both. For something firmer, use *kailangan* (need, have to). Compare: *Dapat kang matulog* (you should sleep) versus *Kailangan mong matulog* (you need to sleep).
**Kaya means "able"** and is said *KA-ya*. Don't confuse it with *ka-YA* ("so") from unit 15. *Kaya ko* = I can; *Kaya mo iyan!* = you can do it! — the most typical Filipino words of encouragement.

**Nang marami** uses *nang* (spelled n-a-n-g) to mark manner. It's a different word from the marker *ng*, though they sound exactly alike: *nang* for manner and time, *ng* for marking things. Even native speakers often mix up the spelling.
**Mas mura** uses *mas* (from Spanish) to compare: *mas mura* (cheaper), *mas malaki* (bigger), *mas mabuti* (better). The superlative uses *pinaka-*: *pinakamura* (cheapest).
**Fit lang, ha** — Taglish again, and again the particle *ha* turning a denial into a joke.

grammars.title: Five words and their pronouns
body: These words aren't full verbs: they have no aspect and never change form. Only the verb that follows them changes.
after: The verb that follows is always in the **infinitive** — the basic form without aspect: *kumain*, *mag-aral*, *matulog*, *umalis*. Never *kumakain* or *nag-aral*.
A linker is required between the pronoun and the verb: *gusto **kong** kumain*, *dapat **kang** matulog*, *puwede **akong** umalis*. The same *-ng* linker as in unit 3.
To negate, put *hindi* in front: *Hindi ko gusto* (I don't like it — though *ayaw ko* is more common), *Hindi ko kailangan* (I don't need it), *Hindi puwede* (not allowed).

grammars.title: A thing or an action?
body: This is the part that goes wrong most. Notice that the marker changes, not the word.

head: What you want
Pattern
Example
Translation
rows: I don't want to get fat.

after: The third row hides a subtle lesson: *gusto ko ng kape* means "I want coffee" (any coffee), while *gusto ko ang kape* means "I like this coffee" or "I like coffee" in general, as something you enjoy. The *ng* / *ang* difference here is exactly the focus difference from unit 13.
*Gusto kita* means "I like you" — using the combined form *kita* you know from unit 4. Use it with care: it's fairly close to a declaration of love.
To offer something, use the question form: *Gusto mo ba ng kape?* — "would you like coffee?" The most standard host's line in the Philippines.

blocks.text: **Bawal** is worth learning separately because it's everywhere on signs: *bawal umihi dito* (no urinating here), *bawal pumasok* (no entry), *bawal tumawid* (no crossing). It's one of the first words newcomers to Manila pick up.

blocks.title: Saying no without offending
items: A flat *ayaw ko* sounds rather harsh in Filipino culture. Softer: *Sige, sa susunod na lang po.* ("Maybe next time.")
Declining food: *Busog pa po ako, salamat.* ("I'm still full, thank you.") Your host will offer once or twice more — that's etiquette, not real pressure.

blocks.text: *Kaysa sa* shortens to *kaysa* in conversation, and often disappears entirely when the comparison is clear from context: *Mas gusto ko ito.* — "I prefer this one."
